claims.text: Melt spinning followed by short annealing will simultaneously increase strength and ductility relative to conventional casting.
Rapid solidification refines the eutectic lamellar architecture.
Post-solidification annealing promotes controlled nanoprecipitate decoration at phase interfaces.
The conventional-cast baseline has coarse lamellar spacing and a homogeneous phase distribution.
Melt spinning can provide a cooling rate on the order of 10^5 K/s.
Annealing at 800°C for 5 minutes in an inert atmosphere will enable controlled nanoprecipitate formation at lamellar interfaces.
A cooling rate of approximately 10^5 K/s suppresses coarse eutectic-colony formation.
Annealing at 800°C for 5 minutes permits nanoprecipitate development without substantial coarsening.
The treatment produces ultrafine lamellar spacing with nanoscale precipitates decorating phase boundaries.
Microstructural refinement increases yield strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
The nanoprecipitates increase yield strength through Orowan strengthening.
Coherent, well-distributed interfaces promote more uniform plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation delays crack initiation and propagation and thereby improves ductility.
The treatment will increase yield strength by approximately 20–30% relative to the conventional-cast alloy.
The treatment will increase tensile elongation by approximately 10–20% relative to the conventional-cast alloy.
Failure to achieve the required cooling rate can cause incomplete microstructural refinement.
Deviation from the specified annealing duration can lead to deleterious phase formation.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements depends on alloy composition.
